title: The 1950s albums and chronology
summary: He lists the flute sonata, quartets, the New York suite, 'By George' and 'Handyland, U.S.A.'

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Perhaps we should get back to that work.
Back to the work, yes. The Label X material, for example. The saxophone quartets that I had written.
I'm sort of lost in the chronology there. After the Raeburn band and perhaps during this misty period, at what point did you begin working again seriously?
When did the saxophone quartet come and the ten piece band; what was the sequence there?
I wrote the flute and piano sonata in the fifties, when I was doing most of this work--'51, '52. I wrote three separate quartets, one suite--saxophone suite.
In '54 I did the "By George" album for Label X, and I did the four altos album for Zoot, I think the following year.
The first one was a kind of an all jazz thing, most of it was the usual chord structures.
What was the name of it?
"Handyland, U.S.A." That was mostly first choruses, and individual choruses by the guys and a final statement. They were all like that.

A reflection of the standardized jazz of the day, which brought about the second album, when I had a completely free hand and I decided to try for some new jazz forms, some new structures; that's what the second album was based on. That's the one that I felt I did some important things.
